# La Poupée: A Comprehensive Analysis of Hans Bellmer's Artistic Project

## Creation and Construction of the Dolls

Hans Bellmer's seminal artistic project, *La Poupée* (The Doll), originated in Berlin during the tumultuous early 1930s, a period marked by profound political instability and personal crisis , . The creation of the dolls was not merely an artistic endeavor but a deeply personal and politically charged act of construction, born from a confluence of familial anxieties, artistic influences, and a burgeoning ideological opposition to the rising Nazi regime , . Bellmer began constructing his first articulated doll in 1933, the very year Adolf Hitler became Chancellor of Germany, and he formally severed ties with his father, who supported the Nazis, around the same time , . This timing underscores the work's dual genesis as both a private therapeutic tool and a public statement of dissent . His motivation was explicitly rooted in his reaction against the aesthetic and ideological conformity promoted by fascism; he sought to create an object that embodied disruption, fragmentation, and erotic perversity, thereby subverting the ideal of the whole, healthy, and pure Aryan body , . The initial catalyst for the project is traced to a series of specific events in 1932, including a visit from his cousin Ursula Naguschewski, his mother sending him her own toy box, and his attendance at Jacques Offenbach’s opera *Tales of Hoffmann*, which explores themes of artificial life and obsession , . Concurrently, Bellmer was grappling with illness within his family, including a tuberculosis diagnosis for his wife and an illness for his father, which contributed to a heightened state of anxiety and provided a context for his artistic catharsis .

The first iteration of *La Poupée* was constructed in 1933-1934, often in collaboration with his younger brother Fritz, a trained engineer, and sometimes with his wife Margarete , , . This initial figure was a life-sized representation of an adolescent girl, standing approximately fifty-six inches tall , . Its construction involved a complex assembly of disparate materials designed to achieve a specific uncanny effect. The internal structure consisted of a wooden armature, reinforced with metal, covered partially with flax fiber , , . The outer shell was formed from plaster and glue, with some sources also mentioning papier mâché and straw , , . The surface was finished with a masklike head featuring glass eyes and a long, unkempt wig, and its limbs were made from broomsticks or dowel rods , . A system of ball-joints allowed for extensive mobility and disturbing configurations, enabling the doll to be posed in contorted and disarticulated ways , . One source describes a more elaborate version of this first doll, constructed from wood, metal, and plaster, which included an innovative feature of internal panoramas viewable through the doll's stomach via a button on its nipple; however, this mechanism proved too cumbersome and was ultimately abandoned in favor of a simpler design . The completed doll was described by Bellmer as a "real object to be possessed," intended not just as a subject for photography but as a fetish object in its own right , .

Following the success of his first doll, Bellmer developed a second, more sophisticated and modular version between 1935 and 1938 , , . This new creation represented a significant evolution in both concept and technical execution. Inspired by sixteenth-century articulated wooden dolls housed in Berlin’s Kaiser Friedrich Museum, Bellmer designed a central spherical ball joint located at the doll's exposed abdomen , . This universal joint was the mechanical heart of the second doll, enabling full articulation and allowing for the interchangeability of various body parts , . The resulting configurations could be non-mimetic "anagrams" of the human body, moving beyond simple fragmentation into more abstract and unsettling arrangements . For instance, Plate 9 from one of his publications shows two sets of hips and legs radiating from the central belly, while Plate 12 features a reversed pelvis substituted for the chest, giving the figure buttocks for breasts . This doll could be configured with four legs, four stylized breasts, multiple torsos, and three different pelvises, all mounted on a single armature . Notably, Bellmer reused the head and hand from the first doll in this second series, creating a sense of continuity and recycling within his project . The overall appearance of the second doll was smoother and more artificial-looking than its predecessor, reinforcing its status as a constructed, man-made object rather than a representation of organic flesh . This second, more advanced doll was the primary subject of the over 100 hand-colored photographs that would later cement Bellmer's reputation . The creation of these dolls was thus a deliberate process of engineering and assembly, reflecting Bellmer's description of his body configurations as a "plastic anagram" .

## Photographic Series and Publication History

The visual documentation of Hans Bellmer's dolls through photography is arguably the most crucial component of the *La Poupée* project, transforming the physical sculptures into a powerful and enduring body of imagery . Beginning almost immediately after the completion of his first doll in 1934, Bellmer embarked on a prolific photographic campaign, producing approximately thirty black-and-white gelatin silver prints , . These initial photographs were staged in a variety of settings, ranging from static studio still lifes that documented the construction process itself to provocative tableaux set within domestic interiors such as basements and haylofts , . The lighting was often chiaroscuro, emphasizing theatrical contrasts and casting deep shadows that enhanced the doll's uncanny quality . Many of these early images were nude, save for a hair bow or patent-leather shoes, and frequently posed the figure as a victim of sexual attack or physical abuse, exploring themes of fetishism and sadism , . A key characteristic of Bellmer's photographic style was its minimalism and reliance on visual autonomy. He often arranged seductive props alongside the doll, such as a black veil, eyelet undergarments, or an artificial rose, but he deliberately avoided providing any explanatory text or captions to accompany the images , . This approach aligned perfectly with the core principles of the Surrealist movement, which valued the image's ability to generate its own autonomous meaning and evoke "convulsive beauty" without rational explanation , .

Bellmer's work gained international prominence through a series of pivotal publications. The first major exposure occurred with the publication of ten photographs from his book *Die Puppe* (The Doll) in the Winter 1934–1935 edition (No. 6) of the influential Parisian surrealist magazine *Le Minotaure* , , . The photographs were presented under the subtitle 'Variations sur le montage d’une mineure articulée' ('Variations on the assembly of an articulated minor') and appeared without any accompanying text, a curatorial choice that underscored their purely visual impact , , . This appearance in *Minotaure*, founded by Albert Skira and edited by figures like André Breton, launched Bellmer into the Parisian avant-garde scene and earned the enthusiastic endorsement of the Surrealist leader himself , . Following this breakthrough, Bellmer continued to develop his second, more modular doll and multiplied his photographic sessions, documenting over 100 new compositions , . These later photographs showed a shift from static documentation to more narrative-driven scenes with sinister, character-driven elements . Some images even incorporated a voyeuristic male figure, such as Bellmer's brother in an overcoat, observing the disrobed and reconfigured doll, adding a layer of psychological tension to the tableaux , . Many of these gelatin silver prints were subsequently hand-colored using aniline dyes, applied in theatrical tones or lurid colors reminiscent of turn-of-the-century prurient novelty postcards, further enhancing their dreamlike and unsettling quality , , .

The dissemination of Bellmer's work continued through several important publications that formalized and expanded upon his initial success. His self-published book *Die Puppe*, issued in late 1934, was a landmark achievement that established his authorial control over the presentation of his work , . This was followed by the official French publication of *La Poupée* by GLM in 1936, which featured an introduction written by Bellmer and translated by Robert Valencay , . A more comprehensive volume, *Les Jeux de la poupée* (The Games of the Doll), was published much later, on November 30, 1949, by Éditions Premières . This book paired Bellmer's photographs with fourteen poems by Paul Éluard, whose work was directly inspired by the second doll , . The 1949 publication served as a definitive codification of the series, preparing many of the photographs for print and ensuring their lasting legacy . The photographs themselves vary widely in size and medium, reflecting their production over nearly two decades. Examples include a large-format hand-colored gelatin silver print measuring 101 x 101 cm from 1963, a smaller print of 41 x 32.9 cm from 1949, and numerous other vintage prints held in museum collections worldwide , . Each photograph functions as a discrete unit within a larger thematic exploration of the female body as a site of fantasy, trauma, and political subversion, solidifying Bellmer's place in the history of twentieth-century photography.

## Surrealist Affiliation and Psychoanalytic Framework

Hans Bellmer's work was enthusiastically embraced by the Surrealist movement, particularly by its leader, André Breton, who recognized in *La Poupée* a powerful embodiment of the group's core tenets . Bellmer himself expressed his delight at being considered part of the movement, though he maintained a degree of critical distance, asserting that his works were "always carefully thought out and controlled" rather than being mere expressions of automatic writing or spontaneous irrationality . Despite this nuance, his photographs resonated deeply with the Surrealist interest in fetishism, desire, ambivalence, and the grotesque . The dolls, with their fragmented, reassembled, and eroticized forms, were seen as perfect manifestations of "convulsive beauty"—a term Breton used to describe moments of intense, irrational revelation that shattered conventional perception . The Surrealists were drawn to the mannequin-like quality of the dolls, viewing them as objects that existed at the intersection of the familiar and the strange, capable of unlocking the latent content of the unconscious mind . Bellmer's declaration that the world itself was a "scandal" positioned his work as a form of radical critique, aligning with the movement's broader goals of challenging bourgeois morality and social taboos .

The artistic and theoretical framework of Bellmer's work is firmly rooted in psychoanalysis, especially the theories of Sigmund Freud . Bellmer explicitly approached the female body as a "linguistic game," assembling its constituent parts in variable configurations to reveal unconscious meanings and explore the dynamics of desire . His constructions can be read through the lens of Freudian concepts such as fetishism—the displacement of anxiety onto an inanimate object—and the uncanny (*das Unheimliche*), which describes the unsettling feeling evoked by something that is both familiar and foreign . The dolls' fragmented bodies, with their doubling and rearrangement of anatomical parts, functioned as emblems of the uncanny, blurring the lines between the animate and the inanimate, the real and the artificial , . Bellmer described the second doll as representing the "physical unconscious," a materialization of hidden psychological drives and conflicts . The provocative and often violent tableaux he staged with the dolls explored themes of sadism and masochism, investigating the darker aspects of the human psyche and the power dynamics inherent in the gaze , . By treating the female body as a plastic anagram—a collection of interchangeable parts—he engaged with Freudian ideas about the fluidity and multiplicity of identity, suggesting that the self is not a unified whole but a composite of fragmented desires and anxieties , .

Scholars have extensively analyzed *La Poupée* through psychoanalytic and post-structuralist frameworks, linking it to subsequent theories. For example, Bellmer's work is theoretically connected to Jacques Lacan's concept of 'le corps morcelé' (the fragmented body), which posits that the human subject is inherently divided and incomplete . The dolls, with their disjointed limbs and impossible geometries, serve as a visual representation of this psychic fragmentation. The work is also situated within a broader lineage of dark Romanticism, stretching from Goya and Fuseli to Max Ernst, that explores the subconscious, the evil, and the secret . Bellmer’s fascination with the gloomy and the secretive aligns with this tradition, positioning his dolls as endpoints in a century-long exploration of the irrational and the monstrous . Furthermore, his work engages with Marxist theory, as his critique of the commodified female body can be seen as an analysis of fetishism within a capitalist society . The doll, as a manufactured object designed for possession and consumption, becomes a potent symbol of how desire is shaped and distorted by economic and social forces . This multifaceted engagement with psychoanalytic, literary, and socio-political theories demonstrates that Bellmer's project was far from a simple exercise in shock value; it was a rigorous and sustained investigation into the deepest structures of the human psyche and the cultural forces that shape it.

## Anti-Fascist Resistance and Political Subversion

While often interpreted through a psychoanalytic lens, the creation of *La Poupée* cannot be divorced from its immediate historical and political context: the rise of National Socialism in Germany . Bellmer's work was a direct and defiant response to the fascist ideology that sought to impose rigid norms of bodily purity, racial hygiene, and ideological conformity . The Nazi regime viewed modernist art and culture as morally, mentally, and racially corrupt, labeling it "degenerate art" (*Entartete Kunst*) , . This condemnation was not arbitrary; it targeted movements like Surrealism, Dada, Expressionism, and New Objectivity for their distortion of the human form, psychological intensity, and perceived links to Jewish and Communist influence , . Bellmer’s dolls, with their fragmented, eroticized, and defiantly non-normative bodies, were a direct assault on the very ideals that fascism sought to promote . By presenting a female body that was monstrous, dismembered, and endlessly reconfigurable, Bellmer subverted the Nazi promotion of the whole, healthy, and reproductive Aryan body . His work exposed the fragility and constructedness of bodily identity, offering a powerful antithesis to the biological essentialism of Nazi propaganda .

Consequently, Bellmer's work was officially condemned by the regime. It was classified as *Entartete Kunst* and fell under the category of "insults to German feeling," deemed symptomatic of "mental and physical degeneration" . The 1937 *Degenerate Art* exhibition in Munich, which showcased over 600 confiscated avant-garde works, likely featured Surrealist pieces like Bellmer's, systematically ridiculing them with mocking wall slogans to delegitimize their existence , . The explicit political nature of his project is confirmed by Bellmer's own actions; he cut ties with his Nazi-supporting father in 1933 and vowed to refuse "useful activity" that would aid the regime, framing the creation of the doll as a symbolic rejection of fascist ideals . This political stance forced him to flee Germany in 1938, seeking refuge in Paris where he joined the Surrealist circle and continued his work , . His internment as a German citizen in a French prison camp from 1940 to 1941 further illustrates the precarious position of artists caught between conflicting ideologies during the war .

In recent years, there has been a concerted effort by scholars and institutions to frame Surrealism, and Bellmer's work in particular, explicitly within an anti-fascist context. The 2024–2025 Lenbachhaus exhibition in Munich, titled 'But Live Here? No Thanks: Surrealism and Anti-fascism', provides a significant institutional validation of this reading , . The exhibition explicitly positions Bellmer's fragmented and violated bodies as a multi-pronged strategy of political resistance, demonstrating how Surrealists deployed artistic methods—including distortion and allegory—to confront and critique fascist violence , . Bellmer was included among other German expatriate and interned artists as a central figure in the Surrealist response to fascism in Germany . This curatorial framing moves beyond viewing the work solely as a product of personal psychology or aesthetic innovation and instead situates it as a vital component of a politicized, international movement dedicated to opposing oppression and authoritarianism . The exhibition highlights how Surrealists like Bellmer challenged the fascist glorification of the military body and instead explored the body as a site of trauma, memory, and resistance . By doing so, it reinforces the understanding that the disturbing and perverse qualities of *La Poupée* are inseparable from its radical political charge, making it a cornerstone of anti-fascist artistic practice in the interwar period.

## Critical Reception and Feminist Reinterpretation

From its inception, Hans Bellmer's *La Poupée* has been a subject of intense critical debate, with interpretations evolving significantly over the decades. The most persistent and controversial aspect of the work is its relationship to gender and feminism. Early readings, particularly those from the 1980s and 1990s, often characterized Bellmer's work as inherently misogynistic . Scholars such as Rudolf E. Kuenzli argued that the dolls were representations of the "physical unconscious" that evidenced pedophilic impulses and a desire to distort and dismember the female body . From this perspective, the dolls are seen as the result of male fear of castration and fetishistic disavowals, functioning to secure a traditional conception of the male self by staging the female body as monstrous and fragmented , . Hal Foster similarly noted that Bellmer's work has often been "shunted to the margins even within Surrealism" due to these tendencies . This interpretation views the work as a product of patriarchal anxiety, where the female form is violated and reassembled according to a male fantasy, reinforcing oppressive gender roles. The recurring motifs of the partly dressed or nude doll, often wearing Mary-Jane school shoes and posed provocatively, fit squarely within this framework of male scopophilia , .

However, a significant counter-narrative has emerged in more recent scholarship, particularly following the rise of feminist art history in the late 20th century. This reinterpretation positions Bellmer's work as a foundational "proto-feminist" precursor, whose exploration of bodily fragmentation, trauma, and gendered representation anticipated key concerns of feminist artists in the 1970s and beyond , . A pivotal moment in this re-evaluation was the 2007 MOCA exhibition 'WACK! Art and the Feminist Revolution', which featured Bellmer's *La Poupée* as an influential antecedent to feminist aesthetics , . The exhibition's curatorial framework argued that Bellmer's work should be understood not as a celebration of male dominance, but as a critical interrogation of the female body as a cultural construct. By deconstructing and reassembling the doll, Bellmer exposed the body as an artificial and unstable entity, laying the groundwork for feminist artists like Eleanor Antin, who famously documented her weight-loss journey in a grid of photographs to critique the objectification of women's bodies . In this view, the fragmentation of the doll becomes an act of liberation, breaking down the monolithic and idealized image of femininity to reveal its constructed nature.

This ongoing debate highlights the tension between authorial intent and interpretive reception. While Bellmer's stated motivations were psychoanalytic explorations of his own desires and anxieties, the formal qualities of the work allow for a wide range of readings . Feminist critics argue that the very act of taking apart and re-making the female body, regardless of the creator's intent, can be a radical gesture. The dolls, stripped of their original context and displayed in art institutions, become detached from their presumed authorial message and open to new interpretations. The controversy surrounding *La Poupée* is therefore not a flaw but a testament to its complexity and power. It remains a work that continues to provoke discussion about the relationship between art, gender, sexuality, and politics, forcing viewers to confront uncomfortable questions about desire, power, and representation. This contested legacy ensures its continued relevance in contemporary art discourse, as each generation of scholars and artists re-engages with its unsettling and provocative imagery.

## Legacy, Institutional Presence, and Enduring Significance

Hans Bellmer's *La Poupée* has secured a canonical status within the canon of 20th-century art, exerting a profound and lasting influence on subsequent generations of artists and securing its place in the permanent collections of the world's most prestigious museums , . Its significance extends far beyond its origins in the Berlin Surrealist scene, continuing to resonate in contemporary discussions about the body, identity, and trauma. Major institutions hold substantial holdings of his work, testifying to its recognized importance. The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York possesses several key pieces, including the constructed sculpture 'The Machine-Gunneress in a State of Grace' (1937) and a vintage gelatin silver print album titled *La poupée* (1936) , . The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds a hand-colored gelatin silver print titled 'La Poupée' (1938), accessioned in 2005, as well as another work from 1936 , . The Centre Pompidou in Paris maintains a robust collection of Bellmer's photographs, including multiple hand-colored prints from circa 1935–1936, acquired in the 1980s and 1990s , , . These holdings demonstrate that *La Poupée* is not merely a historical curiosity but a living presence in the museum landscape, continually studied and exhibited.

The work's legacy is further cemented by its inclusion in major thematic exhibitions that trace its influence across the history of art. MoMA's 2004–2005 exhibition 'Exquisite Corpses: Drawing and Disfiguration' positioned Bellmer as a central exemplar of "aberrant figuration," highlighting his contribution to a century-long artistic preoccupation with disfiguration, trauma, and the anxieties projected onto the human body . The exhibition linked his doll-based imagery to a lineage that includes Giorgio de Chirico, Louise Bourgeois, and the Chapman Brothers, underscoring the enduring centrality of the body as a site of artistic inquiry . Similarly, the Städel Museum’s 2012 exhibition 'Dark Romanticism' placed Bellmer's work at the 20th-century endpoint of a tradition that stretches back to Goya, situating his exploration of the gloomy and the evil within a broader European cultural history . These institutional framings ensure that Bellmer's work is continuously contextualized and re-interpreted, connecting his 1930s creations to contemporary artistic practices and ongoing scholarly conversations. His influence can be seen in the work of artists who explore themes of transformation, fragmentation, and the uncanny, carrying forward the legacy of questioning the boundaries between the human and the machine, the organic and the artificial.

In conclusion, Hans Bellmer's *La Poupée* stands as a landmark achievement in modern art, a work of immense complexity and enduring power. Its legacy is defined by its successful fusion of the psychoanalytic and the political, creating a body of work that is simultaneously a personal exploration of desire and a radical act of anti-fascist resistance , . The intricate construction of the dolls and the haunting beauty of the photographs continue to captivate audiences, while the controversies surrounding its interpretation ensure its vitality in academic and artistic discourse , . Whether viewed as a misogynistic fantasy or a proto-feminist deconstruction of gendered identity, *La Poupée* fundamentally challenges our perceptions of the human form and the societal forces that shape it . As Bellmer himself suggested, the world is a scandal, and through his provocative and meticulously crafted dolls, he created a mirror that reflects its fractured and contradictory essence. The continued presence of his work in major collections and its inclusion in influential exhibitions confirm that *La Poupée* is not a relic of the past but a vital and relevant force in the ongoing conversation about art, politics, and the human condition.

Each photograph functions as a discrete unit within a larger thematic exploration of the female body as a site of fantasy, trauma, and political subversion, solidifying Bellmer's place in the history of twentieth-century photography.
The self-published book *Die Puppe* was published in late 1934.
The self-published book *Die Puppe* featured ten photographs of the first doll.
The self-published book *Die Puppe* established Bellmer's authorial voice and control.
*Minotaure* No. 6 was published in Winter 1934–1935.
*Minotaure* No. 6 featured a landmark appearance of 18 photographs from the first doll series.
*Minotaure* No. 6 was published without explanatory text, launching Bellmer internationally.
*La Poupée* (French Edition) was published in 1936.
*La Poupée* (French Edition) was the official French edition published by GLM, featuring an introduction by Bellmer.
*Les Jeux de la poupée* was published on November 30, 1949.
*Les Jeux de la poupée* was the final and most comprehensive publication, pairing Bellmer's photographs with poems by Paul Éluard.
Hans Bellmer's work was enthusiastically embraced by the Surrealist movement, particularly by its leader, André Breton, who recognized in *La Poupée* a powerful embodiment of the group's core tenets.

Bellmer himself expressed his delight at being considered part of the movement, though he maintained a degree of critical distance, asserting that his works were "always carefully thought out and controlled" rather than being mere expressions of automatic writing or spontaneous irrationality.
Despite this nuance, Bellmer's photographs resonated deeply with the Surrealist interest in fetishism, desire, ambivalence, and the grotesque.

The dolls, with their fragmented, reassembled, and eroticized forms, were seen as perfect manifestations of "convulsive beauty"—a term Breton used to describe moments of intense, irrational revelation that shattered conventional perception.

The Surrealists were drawn to the mannequin-like quality of the dolls, viewing them as objects that existed at the intersection of the familiar and the strange, capable of unlocking the latent content of the unconscious mind.

Bellmer's declaration that the world itself was a "scandal" positioned his work as a form of radical critique, aligning with the movement's broader goals of challenging bourgeois morality and social taboos.
The artistic and theoretical framework of Bellmer's work is firmly rooted in psychoanalysis, especially the theories of Sigmund Freud.
Bellmer explicitly approached the female body as a "linguistic game," assembling its constituent parts in variable configurations to reveal unconscious meanings and explore the dynamics of desire.

Bellmer's constructions can be read through the lens of Freudian concepts such as fetishism—the displacement of anxiety onto an inanimate object—and the uncanny (*das Unheimliche*), which describes the unsettling feeling evoked by something that is both familiar and foreign.

The dolls' fragmented bodies, with their doubling and rearrangement of anatomical parts, functioned as emblems of the uncanny, blurring the lines between the animate and the inanimate, the real and the artificial.
Bellmer described the second doll as representing the "physical unconscious," a materialization of hidden psychological drives and conflicts.

The provocative and often violent tableaux Bellmer staged with the dolls explored themes of sadism and masochism, investigating the darker aspects of the human psyche and the power dynamics inherent in the gaze.

By treating the female body as a plastic anagram—a collection of interchangeable parts—Bellmer engaged with Freudian ideas about the fluidity and multiplicity of identity, suggesting that the self is not a unified whole but a composite of fragmented desires and anxieties.
Scholars have extensively analyzed *La Poupée* through psychoanalytic and post-structuralist frameworks, linking it to subsequent theories.
Bellmer's work is theoretically connected to Jacques Lacan's concept of 'le corps morcelé' (the fragmented body), which posits that the human subject is inherently divided and incomplete.
The dolls, with their disjointed limbs and impossible geometries, serve as a visual representation of this psychic fragmentation.
The work is also situated within a broader lineage of dark Romanticism, stretching from Goya and Fuseli to Max Ernst, that explores the subconscious, the evil, and the secret.
Bellmer’s fascination with the gloomy and the secretive aligns with this tradition, positioning his dolls as endpoints in a century-long exploration of the irrational and the monstrous.
Bellmer's work engages with Marxist theory, as his critique of the commodified female body can be seen as an analysis of fetishism within a capitalist society.
The doll, as a manufactured object designed for possession and consumption, becomes a potent symbol of how desire is shaped and distorted by economic and social forces.

This multifaceted engagement with psychoanalytic, literary, and socio-political theories demonstrates that Bellmer's project was far from a simple exercise in shock value; it was a rigorous and sustained investigation into the deepest structures of the human psyche and the cultural forces that shape it.
While often interpreted through a psychoanalytic lens, the creation of *La Poupée* cannot be divorced from its immediate historical and political context: the rise of National Socialism in Germany.
Bellmer's work was a direct and defiant response to the fascist ideology that sought to impose rigid norms of bodily purity, racial hygiene, and ideological conformity.
The Nazi regime viewed modernist art and culture as morally, mentally, and racially corrupt, labeling it "degenerate art" (*Entartete Kunst*).

This condemnation was not arbitrary; it targeted movements like Surrealism, Dada, Expressionism, and New Objectivity for their distortion of the human form, psychological intensity, and perceived links to Jewish and Communist influence.
Bellmer’s dolls, with their fragmented, eroticized, and defiantly non-normative bodies, were a direct assault on the very ideals that fascism sought to promote.
By presenting a female body that was monstrous, dismembered, and endlessly reconfigurable, Bellmer subverted the Nazi promotion of the whole, healthy, and reproductive Aryan body.
Bellmer's work exposed the fragility and constructedness of bodily identity, offering a powerful antithesis to the biological essentialism of Nazi propaganda.
Consequently, Bellmer's work was officially condemned by the regime.
Bellmer's work was classified as *Entartete Kunst* and fell under the category of "insults to German feeling," deemed symptomatic of "mental and physical degeneration."

The 1937 *Degenerate Art* exhibition in Munich, which showcased over 600 confiscated avant-garde works, likely featured Surrealist pieces like Bellmer's, systematically ridiculing them with mocking wall slogans to delegitimize their existence.

The explicit political nature of Bellmer's project is confirmed by his own actions; he cut ties with his Nazi-supporting father in 1933 and vowed to refuse "useful activity" that would aid the regime, framing the creation of the doll as a symbolic rejection of fascist ideals.
This political stance forced Bellmer to flee Germany in 1938, seeking refuge in Paris where he joined the Surrealist circle and continued his work.
Bellmer's internment as a German citizen in a French prison camp from 1940 to 1941 further illustrates the precarious position of artists caught between conflicting ideologies during the war.
In recent years, there has been a concerted effort by scholars and institutions to frame Surrealism, and Bellmer's work in particular, explicitly within an anti-fascist context.
The 2024–2025 Lenbachhaus exhibition in Munich, titled 'But Live Here? No Thanks: Surrealism and Anti-fascism', provides a significant institutional validation of this reading.

The exhibition explicitly positions Bellmer's fragmented and violated bodies as a multi-pronged strategy of political resistance, demonstrating how Surrealists deployed artistic methods—including distortion and allegory—to confront and critique fascist violence.
Bellmer was included among other German expatriate and interned artists as a central figure in the Surrealist response to fascism in Germany.

This curatorial framing moves beyond viewing the work solely as a product of personal psychology or aesthetic innovation and instead situates it as a vital component of a politicized, international movement dedicated to opposing oppression and authoritarianism.
The exhibition highlights how Surrealists like Bellmer challenged the fascist glorification of the military body and instead explored the body as a site of trauma, memory, and resistance.

By doing so, it reinforces the understanding that the disturbing and perverse qualities of *La Poupée* are inseparable from its radical political charge, making it a cornerstone of anti-fascist artistic practice in the interwar period.
From its inception, Hans Bellmer's *La Poupée* has been a subject of intense critical debate, with interpretations evolving significantly over the decades.
The most persistent and controversial aspect of the work is its relationship to gender and feminism.
Early readings, particularly those from the 1980s and 1990s, often characterized Bellmer's work as inherently misogynistic.
Scholars such as Rudolf E. Kuenzli argued that the dolls were representations of the "physical unconscious" that evidenced pedophilic impulses and a desire to distort and dismember the female body.

From this perspective, the dolls are seen as the result of male fear of castration and fetishistic disavowals, functioning to secure a traditional conception of the male self by staging the female body as monstrous and fragmented.
Hal Foster similarly noted that Bellmer's work has often been "shunted to the margins even within Surrealism" due to these tendencies.
This interpretation views the work as a product of patriarchal anxiety, where the female form is violated and reassembled according to a male fantasy, reinforcing oppressive gender roles.
The recurring motifs of the partly dressed or nude doll, often wearing Mary-Jane school shoes and posed provocatively, fit squarely within this framework of male scopophilia.
A significant counter-narrative has emerged in more recent scholarship, particularly following the rise of feminist art history in the late 20th century.

This reinterpretation positions Bellmer's work as a foundational "proto-feminist" precursor, whose exploration of bodily fragmentation, trauma, and gendered representation anticipated key concerns of feminist artists in the 1970s and beyond.
A pivotal moment in this re-evaluation was the 2007 MOCA exhibition 'WACK! Art and the Feminist Revolution', which featured Bellmer's *La Poupée* as an influential antecedent to feminist aesthetics.

The exhibition's curatorial framework argued that Bellmer's work should be understood not as a celebration of male dominance, but as a critical interrogation of the female body as a cultural construct.

By deconstructing and reassembling the doll, Bellmer exposed the body as an artificial and unstable entity, laying the groundwork for feminist artists like Eleanor Antin, who famously documented her weight-loss journey in a grid of photographs to critique the objectification of women's bodies.
In this view, the fragmentation of the doll becomes an act of liberation, breaking down the monolithic and idealized image of femininity to reveal its constructed nature.
This ongoing debate highlights the tension between authorial intent and interpretive reception.
While Bellmer's stated motivations were psychoanalytic explorations of his own desires and anxieties, the formal qualities of the work allow for a wide range of readings.
Feminist critics argue that the very act of taking apart and re-making the female body, regardless of the creator's intent, can be a radical gesture.
The dolls, stripped of their original context and displayed in art institutions, become detached from their presumed authorial message and open to new interpretations.
The controversy surrounding *La Poupée* is not a flaw but a testament to its complexity and power.

It remains a work that continues to provoke discussion about the relationship between art, gender, sexuality, and politics, forcing viewers to confront uncomfortable questions about desire, power, and representation.
This contested legacy ensures its continued relevance in contemporary art discourse, as each generation of scholars and artists re-engages with its unsettling and provocative imagery.

Hans Bellmer's *La Poupée* has secured a canonical status within the canon of 20th-century art, exerting a profound and lasting influence on subsequent generations of artists and securing its place in the permanent collections of the world's most prestigious museums.
Its significance extends far beyond its origins in the Berlin Surrealist scene, continuing to resonate in contemporary discussions about the body, identity, and trauma.
Major institutions hold substantial holdings of Bellmer's work, testifying to its recognized importance.

The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York possesses several key pieces, including the constructed sculpture 'The Machine-Gunneress in a State of Grace' (1937) and a vintage gelatin silver print album titled *La poupée* (1936).
The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds a hand-colored gelatin silver print titled 'La Poupée' (1938), accessioned in 2005, as well as another work from 1936.
The Centre Pompidou in Paris maintains a robust collection of Bellmer's photographs, including multiple hand-colored prints from circa 1935–1936, acquired in the 1980s and 1990s.
These holdings demonstrate that *La Poupée* is not merely a historical curiosity but a living presence in the museum landscape, continually studied and exhibited.
The work's legacy is further cemented by its inclusion in major thematic exhibitions that trace its influence across the history of art.

MoMA's 2004–2005 exhibition 'Exquisite Corpses: Drawing and Disfiguration' positioned Bellmer as a central exemplar of "aberrant figuration," highlighting his contribution to a century-long artistic preoccupation with disfiguration, trauma, and the anxieties projected onto the human body.

The exhibition linked Bellmer's doll-based imagery to a lineage that includes Giorgio de Chirico, Louise Bourgeois, and the Chapman Brothers, underscoring the enduring centrality of the body as a site of artistic inquiry.

The Städel Museum’s 2012 exhibition 'Dark Romanticism' placed Bellmer's work at the 20th-century endpoint of a tradition that stretches back to Goya, situating his exploration of the gloomy and the evil within a broader European cultural history.

These institutional framings ensure that Bellmer's work is continuously contextualized and re-interpreted, connecting his 1930s creations to contemporary artistic practices and ongoing scholarly conversations.

Bellmer's influence can be seen in the work of artists who explore themes of transformation, fragmentation, and the uncanny, carrying forward the legacy of questioning the boundaries between the human and the machine, the organic and the artificial.
Hans Bellmer's *La Poupée* stands as a landmark achievement in modern art, a work of immense complexity and enduring power.

Its legacy is defined by its successful fusion of the psychoanalytic and the political, creating a body of work that is simultaneously a personal exploration of desire and a radical act of anti-fascist resistance.

The intricate construction of the dolls and the haunting beauty of the photographs continue to captivate audiences, while the controversies surrounding its interpretation ensure its vitality in academic and artistic discourse.

Whether viewed as a misogynistic fantasy or a proto-feminist deconstruction of gendered identity, *La Poupée* fundamentally challenges our perceptions of the human form and the societal forces that shape it.
As Bellmer himself suggested, the world is a scandal, and through his provocative and meticulously crafted dolls, he created a mirror that reflects its fractured and contradictory essence.

The continued presence of Bellmer's work in major collections and its inclusion in influential exhibitions confirm that *La Poupée* is not a relic of the past but a vital and relevant force in the ongoing conversation about art, politics, and the human condition.

Abstract
--------

'This book is platypus-like, unclassifiable.' - Marina Warner, London Review of Books + Since the 19th century, dolls have served as toys but also as objects of obsession, love, and lust. That century witnessed the emergence of the term 'heterosexual' and of modern concepts of fetishism, perversity, and animism. Their convergence, and the demands of a growing consumer society resulted in a proliferation of waxworks, shop-window dummies, and customized love dolls, which also began to appear in art. Oskar Kokoschka commissioned a life-sized doll of his former lover Alma Mahler; Hans Bellmer crafted poupées; and Marcel Duchamp fabricated a nude figure in his environmental tableau Etant donnés. The Erotic Doll is the first book to explore men's complex relationships with such inanimate forms from historical, theoretical, and phenomenological perspectives. Challenging our commonsense grasp of the relations between persons and things, Marquard Smith examines these erotically charged human figures by interweaving art history, visual culture, gender, and sexuality studies with the medical humanities, offering startling insights into heterosexual masculinity and its discontents.

Introduction/Chapter 1. : The Dynamics of Affects and Experiences of the More- and Other-than-Human Bodies When eroticism and sex are discussed, the attention most often focuses on what takes place between people. In this work, the erotic spectacle is more comprehensive and features non-human actors: things, stuff, objects. I set out from the assumption that objects, such as clothing, undergarments, footwear, and jewellery play an important role in stimulating erotic imagination, becoming participants in that process. The theoretical foundation for acknowledging things as active contributors to social relationships (as one should approach amorous-erotic-sexual relationships) derives from the anthropology of things. This perspective is also tangibly present in my analyses, since I seek to show the (post)human, transversal, liminal bodies as they become fused with other—animate and inanimate—bodies and objects. The attribute of “more- and other-than-human” in the title refers to the human, but a human construed in accordance with the concepts posited by the posthuman, new materialism and anthropology of things; an entity functioning in complex networks that link them inseparably with other beings: things, objects, animals, plants, sand, or water. Chapter 2. More-than-human Network of Relationality In this chapter I present theoretical and methodological issues. I show that research, generally referred as study of things, functions in different contexts. The baseline standpoint adopted by Daniel Miller, Peter Pells, Ikuya Tokoro and Kari Kawai is that of social sciences and anthropology, whereas Donna J. Haraway, Bruno Latour, and Rosi Braidotti take into account the outcomes of advances in science, biomedical ones in particular, as well as examine languages and images we employ to convey them. Natural sciences, medicine and biotechnology have long questioned the traditional conceptions of the human as a being apart with respect to other forms of life. Although the main research perspective in this chapter is anthropology of things, I also present here the issues developed in the framework of new materialism, posthumanism and transhumanism. Chapter 3. Nature as a Phantasm of Culture In this chapter I focus on the ambivalence of the duality ‘animal sex – human erotica’. I depart from such clear-cut oppositions which juxtapose the animal against the human, nature against culture, and the normative against the non-normative. This owes to reflection inspired by the ideas of the posthuman, new materialism and the concept of posthuman sexuality which grew out of that intellectual background. In the perspective I have adopted, the dichotomy of “animal sex” versus “human eroticism” is hardly tenable. One can still track down and deconstruct such notions as well as suggest new ways of conceiving and presenting the complex relationships between the human and the non-human, or else still—to portray the sphere of eroticism within a nexus of manifold, non-binary but yet mutable, networked relations. What does not reveal directly returns in secret form: in costumes, utility items, design and eaten products. Chapter 4. The Obsession of Artificial Bodies The heroes and heroines of this chapter are: mannequins, dolls, androids, cyborgs from literature and science fiction. I showed the gender context of those phenomena, as I am convinced that the aesthetic paragons of male and female physiques with their erotic overtones enact certain models of social relationships, and thus impose roles to be performed due to gender. Stories, novels, films – these are the areas of analysis of this chapter. Analyzing various literary, film, art works, I ask about the attitude of people to technology: its potential, limitations, entanglement in new forms of discrimination and oppression. Chapter 5. The “Beloved” Objects This chapter looks at things closest to one’s body (in the literal sense): clothes, underwear, footwear and considers the affects engendered by those objects. These roles are perpetuated (and much less often undermined) not only by dedicated systems of laws, morality, and customs, but also by a plethora of items, things, and objects by means of which we assume certain roles. The main category organizing the analysis of eroticism and sexuality in this approach is “obscenity”. I show ambivalent and related this term in the contemporary culture. Conclusion/ Chapter 6. This work is concerned with bodies, items, and substances in the material sense, as well as in the relationships between humans and nonhumans, other-than-humans, more-than-humans. The ties and associations with the things we produce, use, watch, and touch are by no means straightforward and limited to mere functionality. I perceive them rather as complex relationships of interwoven ingenuity, impulses, and affects. The goal I strove to accomplish was to show that in the erotic sphere the relationships are multilayered and exceedingly intricate. The eroticism of arch-non-human bodies spans affects and conscious modes of (self)creation, while things, objects do take part in these “dealings”. In the afterword, I showed that thinking about our-human, relationships with stuff, objects, and no human, more-than-human, finding non-human in ourselves, opens up new cognitive, emotional and social/community perspectives.

Within La Specola Museum in Florence, Italy, there are several rooms dedicated to the study of human anatomy as understood by the scientific community at the latter end of the 1700s. The anatomical wax figures were created by artisans working for the museum and amongst them are female anatomical sculptural figures, often referred to as Anatomical Venuses, which provide a substantial survey of the maternal body describing the chronology of gestation and birth. Traditional feminist response has highlighted the eroticism of these Anatomical Venuses and the inferior position of woman as the passive object of the male gaze. However, when viewed in vivo, it is evident that the artefacts are much more than objects for male voyeurism.
